Athanasius and Basil

History and saints · Saints

St. Athanasius and St. Basil

4 sectionsNot completed
Notes

Church Fathers are early Christian teachers whose writings form important witnesses to the Church’s faith. St. Athanasius explains the saving purpose of the Incarnation; St. Basil explains the relationship between written teaching and apostolic tradition. Their arguments address different subjects and should be understood in their own texts.[1][2]

What does St. Athanasius say the Incarnation accomplishes?[1]

St. Athanasius argues that the Word’s human life and works make the invisible God known. Christ becomes human for humanity’s salvation and brings the hope of immortality through his death. The passage’s language about humanity being made divine belongs to this account of receiving life from God through the Incarnation.[1]

Read original passage

Athanasius: the Incarnation

As, then, if a man should wish to see God, Who is invisible by nature and not seen at all, he may know and apprehend Him from His works: so let him who fails to see Christ with his understanding, at least apprehend Him by the works of His body, and test whether they be human works or God’s works. 2. And if they be human, let him scoff; but if they are not human, but of God, let him recognise it, and not laugh at what is no matter for scoffing; but rather let him marvel that by so ordinary a means things divine have been manifested to us, and that by death immortality has reached to all, and that by the Word becoming man, the universal Providence has been known, and its Giver and Artificer the very Word of God. 3. For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality.

How does St. Basil describe apostolic tradition?[2]

St. Basil distinguishes teaching received in writing from practices and beliefs transmitted through apostolic tradition. He treats both as significant for the Church’s faith and worship. His argument concerns what the Church has received, rather than a general approval of every later custom.[2]

Read original passage

Basil: Scripture and tradition

Of the beliefs and practices whether generally accepted or publicly enjoined which are preserved in the Church some we possess derived from written teaching; others we have received delivered to us “in a mystery” by the tradition of the apostles; and both of these in relation to true religion have the same force. And these no one will gainsay;—no one, at all events, who is even moderately versed in the institutions of the Church. For were we to attempt to reject such customs as have no written authority, on the ground that the importance they possess is small, we should unintentionally injure the Gospel in its very vitals; or, rather, should make our public definition a mere phrase and nothing more.

St. Athanasius’s complete argument[1]

The linked treatise places chapter 54 within St. Athanasius’s larger account of the Word becoming human. It provides the surrounding reasoning behind the short passage about revelation and immortality.[1]
